chief_complaint: progressive gravelly hoarseness for 4 weeks in heavy smoker
hpi_details: A 65-year-old male presents to the clinic with progressive gravelly hoarseness for 4 weeks in heavy smoker. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he just strained his voice shouting at a recent football match on top of his usual morning smoker's cough.
concerns: He is worried that his decades of smoking have finally caught up with him and caused throat cancer.
expectations: He hopes for a quick camera exam down his throat to see what is going on and a medication to soothe his vocal cords.

investigation_events.title: Urgent office flexible laryngoscopy
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent office flexible laryngoscopy findings are now available.

results.value: Irregular exophytic lesion on the right true vocal cord with reduced cord mobility; airway remains patent
results.note: Requires tissue diagnosis; no pathology result is available during this encounter

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Laryngeal Cancer is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes prompt flexible laryngoscopy with vocal cord biopsy and staging CT of the neck, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Chronic laryngitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

must_ask.say: How many weeks has your voice been hoarse, and is it worsening?

history.answer: My voice has been sounding really rough and gravelly for the past four weeks, and it just keeps getting worse.
It started about four weeks ago and has been gradually deepening and turning raspy without letting up.
It started slowly rather than overnight, and it has been steadily getting more gravelly every week without any good days.
It sounds rough, low-pitched, and gravelly, almost like I am constantly straining to push words out.
Resting my voice does not help at all; it sounds just as harsh and raspy even after sleeping all night.
No, I do not sing, give speeches, or yell; I have been retired and mostly talk quietly at home.
No, I have not had a cold, runny nose, fever, or sore throat recently.
No, I do not get heartburn, chest burning, or sour fluid backing up into my throat.
I feel an annoying irritation in my throat like I need to clear it, but no severe pain.
My breathing is fine right now, and I have not noticed any whistling or harsh sounds when I inhale.
I can swallow food and drinks without trouble, and it does not hurt when I swallow.
No, I do not have any ear pain or pain shooting up to my ears.
I have not noticed any lumps or swellings on either side of my neck.
I have lost about 3 kilograms over the past month without trying, and I have been feeling unusually tired.
I have a slight dry cough from time to time, but I have never coughed up any blood or phlegm.
I have never had surgery on my neck, thyroid, or chest, and I have never been intubated.
No, I do not have chest pain, back pain, or any heart conditions.
No, I do not choke on water, my speech is clear, and I have no weakness, tremor, or eyelid drooping.
I have never used steroid inhalers or nose sprays.
I smoke one pack of cigarettes every day and have done so for 40 years.
I only have a beer or two with friends once or twice a month.
No, I have not been sensitive to the cold, nor have I noticed constipation or dry skin.
I figured I just strained my vocal cords cheering at a football match last month, mixed in with my regular smoker's cough.
Deep down, I'm terrified that after forty years of smoking, this raspy voice means I've got throat cancer.
I'm hoping you can take a look down my throat with a scope today and give me something to get my voice back.
I do not have any diagnosed chronic medical conditions like hypertension or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I am not taking any prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I worked as an office clerk until I retired, and I live at home with my wife.
My father passed away from lung cancer in his sixties, but no one in my family had throat cancer.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.6°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
Comfortable at rest without respiratory distress or audible stridor; speaks with a prominent gravelly, raspy voice.
Oral cavity and pharynx are clear with moist mucosa; no mucosal ulceration, leukoplakia, tonsillar hypertrophy, or mass lesion visible.
No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy along the anterior or posterior cervical chains, and no supraclavicular nodes.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and moves smoothly with swallowing without palpable nodules.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout lung fields without wheezing, crackles, or referred upper airway stridor.
Cranial nerves IX, X, and XII intact; soft palate elevates symmetrically in the midline and tongue protrudes midline without deviation or fasciculations.
